correctness.rationale: A perfect cyclic one-swap code has twenty centers since each radius-one neighborhood has six permutations. The affine subgroup H of order twenty meets each of six ball-translation cosets exactly once, proving existence. Every perfect code is symbol-relabelable to include the identity. Two separately built complete exact-cover programs both visit 41 nodes, find four dead branches, and return exactly one identity-containing code; its complete center set equals H. Thus all and only the six left cosets are perfect. The search branching invariant and all source code are supplied. No infinite extrapolation.

originality.rationale: The foundational 2013 source exhibits H but does not establish uniqueness. A directly overlapping published census gives 3192 maximum ordinary Kendall codes, not the cyclic-perfect subset; the new constraint requires the fifth wraparound swap, and the current theorem excludes all alternatives. No explicitly covering statement was found under the searches and inspected highly relevant primary work, subject to the stated residual risks.
residual_risks: A prior unpublished or unindexed enumeration may have established uniqueness of cyclic-perfect S5 codes.
The published ordinary-code population permits mechanical filtering of its 3192 maxima; it is a close superset, though its stated results do not give the new exact cyclic classification.
The 2016 small-order Kendall article could not be inspected in full; the accessible abstract concerns the ordinary metric.
The classification is completely finite and does not generalize to larger symmetric groups.

value.rationale: The 2013 perfect cyclic Kendall construction motivates a complete determination of whether alternative perfect twenty-word codebooks exist. The theorem rigorously identifies all six designs and proves rigidity up to symbol relabeling. This is a natural complete equality-classification invariant for an established rank-modulation error channel, useful for design and benchmarking, rather than an arbitrary selected subfamily. No general length theorem is claimed.
